hints: Focus on this as a two-stage story, first the hydroxide precipitates, then the effect of adding excess strong acid.
Recall that magnesium hydroxide is an insoluble white solid, while barium hydroxide is soluble in water, so only one mixture gives a precipitate at first.
Now think about sulfate solubilities in excess acid, magnesium sulfate dissolves easily but barium sulfate stays as a very insoluble white solid.
walkthrough:
**First step with NaOH**

Think about which Group 2 hydroxides are insoluble. Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, barium hydroxide is soluble.

Chemical idea:
$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) \text{ colourless solution, no precipitate}$$

**Second step with excess H2SO4 for magnesium**

Strong acid neutralises a base and dissolves the hydroxide precipitate. Magnesium sulfate formed is soluble.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
So the white solid disappears to leave a colourless solution only.

**Second step with excess H2SO4 for barium**

Here sulfate ions meet barium ions. Barium sulfate is famously insoluble, even in excess acid.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$
So at the end you see a white precipitate. That gives colourless solution for magnesium and white precipitate for barium.

options.A: Incorrect. This correctly gives colourless solution for $\text{MgCl}_2$ after the acid dissolves $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, but it wrongly predicts no precipitate for barium. $\text{BaSO}_4$ is insoluble and must precipitate when excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is added.
options.B: Correct. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ white precipitate first forms but then dissolves in excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give soluble $\text{MgSO}_4(aq)$, a colourless solution. $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ stays in solution at first, but addition of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives insoluble white $\text{BaSO}_4(s)$ which remains.
options.C: Incorrect and reversed. Students choosing this forget the second step. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ does precipitate with NaOH, but it is a base and dissolves in excess acid. $\text{BaSO}_4$ does precipitate, so barium cannot end as a colourless solution.
options.D: Incorrect. This describes only the middle of the sequence for magnesium. It is true that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is a white precipitate with NaOH, but the question asks for the end after excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, when it has dissolved to $\text{MgSO}_4(aq)$.
